Sudoku rules
Fill every row, every column and every 3×3 box with the numbers 1 to 9, each exactly once. If you know eight numbers of a group, the ninth is easy!
Look at the blue cell. Its row, column and box are bright. Each of them must contain every number from 1 to 9.
These numbers are already there, so the blue cell can only be %1$d.
Which number goes in the blue cell?
Single candidate
When every number except one is already in a cell\'s row, column or box, that last number must go there.
Look at the blue cell and everything it can \'see\': its row, column and box.
Eight different numbers are already placed there, so only %1$d is left for this cell.
Which number is the only one left for the blue cell?
Hidden single
Sometimes a number has only one place left in a row, column or box — even if that cell still has other candidates.
Focus on the bright group of nine cells and the number %1$d. Where could %1$d go?
Every other empty cell in this group already has a %1$d in its row, column or box, so %1$d can only go in the blue cell.
Number %1$d fits in only one cell of the bright group. Tap that cell.
Pointing pair / triple
If a number\'s candidates inside a box all lie on one line, that number must be in the box part of that line — so remove it from the rest of the line.
In this box, the candidates for %1$d all sit on one line (marked).
The number %1$d must be in one of those cells, so remove it from the other cells of that line (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the marked pattern.
Box-line reduction
If a number\'s candidates in a row or column all lie in one box, that number must be in the line part of the box — remove it from the rest of the box.
In this line, the candidates for %1$d all sit inside one box (marked).
The number %1$d must be in one of those cells, so remove it from the other cells of that box (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the marked pattern.
Naked pair
If two cells in a group have exactly the same two candidates, those two numbers belong to those cells — remove them from the other cells of the group.
These two cells have no candidates other than %1$s.
The numbers %1$s belong to these two cells, so remove them from the other cells of the group (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the marked pair.
Hidden pair
If two numbers can only go in the same two cells of a group, those cells must hold exactly those two numbers — remove their other candidates.
The numbers %1$s fit only in the two marked cells of this group.
These two cells must hold exactly those numbers, so every other candidate in them can be removed (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the hidden pair.
Naked triple
Three cells in a group that together contain only three different candidates must hold exactly those three numbers — remove them from the other cells.
Between them, these three cells use only the numbers %1$s.
The numbers %1$s belong to these three cells, so remove them from the other cells of the group (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the marked triple.
Hidden triple
If three numbers fit only in the same three cells of a group, those cells must hold exactly those numbers — remove their other candidates.
The numbers %1$s fit only in the three marked cells of this group.
These three cells must hold exactly those numbers, so every other candidate in them can be removed (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the hidden triple.
X-Wing

If a number appears as a candidate in exactly two cells in each of two rows, and those cells line up in the same two columns, the number must fill two opposite corners of that rectangle. Remove it from the rest of those columns (or swap rows and columns).
Number %1$d: in each of two lines it has only two candidates, and they line up on the same two crossing lines (the four marked corners).
Number %1$d must take two opposite corners, so it cannot be anywhere else on the two crossing lines (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the X-Wing.
Y-Wing

A pivot cell has two candidates (A, B). One partner that sees the pivot has (A, C); another has (B, C). Whatever the pivot turns out to be, one of the partners must be C — so any cell that sees both partners cannot be C.
The pivot has %1$d and %2$d. One wing has (%1$d, %3$d) and the other has (%2$d, %3$d) — the three marked cells.
If the pivot is %1$d, the second wing is %3$d; if it is %2$d, the first wing is %3$d. Either way one wing is %3$d, so cells that see both wings cannot be %3$d (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the Y-Wing.
Swordfish
Like X-Wing, but with three lines: a number\'s candidates in three lines all fall within the same three crossing lines — remove it from the rest of those crossing lines.
Number %1$d: its candidates in three lines all fall inside the same three crossing lines (marked).
The three lines share the number %1$d across the three crossing lines, so it can be removed from the other cells of those crossing lines (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the Swordfish.

No single number is forced here — a technique is needed. Tap "Learn it" to see which one.
Grandmaster
Master
Skyscraper

Two lines each hold a number in exactly two places, and one end of each lines up in the same column (or row). The other two ends can\'t both be wrong — one of them holds the number — so any cell that sees both of those ends can\'t hold it.
Number %1$d: two lines have it in only two cells each, and one end of each shares a column (or row) — the base. The other two ends, the tips, are marked.
Number %1$d must be in at least one of the two tips, so cells that see both tips cannot hold it (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the Skyscraper.
2-String Kite

A row and a column each hold a number in exactly two cells, and one cell of each sits in the same box. The two far ends can\'t both be wrong — so any cell that sees both far ends can\'t hold the number.
Number %1$d: a row and a column each have it in only two cells, linked through one box (the four marked cells).
One of the two far ends must hold %1$d, so cells that see both far ends cannot (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the 2-String Kite.
XYZ-Wing

A pivot cell with three candidates (X, Y, Z) sees two partner cells: one with (X, Z) and one with (Y, Z). Whatever the pivot turns out to be, Z ends up in the pivot or one of the partners — so a cell that sees all three can\'t be Z.
The pivot has %1$d, %2$d and %3$d. The wings have (%1$d, %3$d) and (%2$d, %3$d) — the three marked cells.
Whichever way it works out, one of the three marked cells is %3$d. Cells that see all three cannot be %3$d (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the XYZ-Wing.
Unique Rectangle

A valid puzzle has exactly one solution. If four cells in two rows, two columns and two boxes could be swapped between the same two numbers, the puzzle would have two solutions — so that pattern must be avoided, which lets you remove candidates.
Three of these four corners hold only %1$s. The fourth corner has those numbers plus others.
If the fourth corner also ended up as %1$s, the puzzle would have two solutions. So those numbers can be removed from it (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the Unique Rectangle.
Simple coloring

Link the cells where a number has only two places in a house, and color them alternately (blue and orange). In each chain exactly one color is true — so cells that see both colors, or two cells of one color that see each other, show what to remove.
Number %1$d: the marked cells form a chain; alternate cells are blue and orange. Exactly one of the two colors holds %1$d.
One color turns out false (two cells of the same color see each other), or a cell sees both colors — so %1$d can be removed there (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the coloring.
XY-Chain

A chain of two-candidate cells where neighbors see each other and share one number. If the chain\'s two ends carry the same number, one end must hold it — so any cell that sees both ends can\'t hold it.
Follow the marked chain: every cell has two candidates and links to the next. Both ends share the number %1$d.
Number %1$d — one end of the chain must hold it, so cells that see both ends cannot (red).
Tap every cell where %1$d can be removed because of the XY-Chain.
